title: YOLO-RoadSurvey: Real-Time Traffic Monitoring and Pavement Damage Detection for Bandung Roadways

authors.name: Andi Kusuma
authors.affiliation: Department of Electrical Engineering, Institut Teknologi Bandung

abstract: Bandung's municipal roads face rapid wear from mixed traffic and heavy rainfall; local authorities need automated, low-cost monitoring to prioritize repairs and manage traffic flow. Existing vision-based road-inspection systems often require heavy GPUs, report accuracy drops below 85% for small cracks, or exhibit latencies exceeding 60 ms on embedded platforms [1]-[5]. We present YOLO-RoadSurvey, a real-time pipeline combining a pruned YOLOv5s detector, a shallow crack segmentation head, and an edge MCU inference node (STM32F407 + Coral Edge TPU accelerator) for continuous roadside deployment. Innovations include (1) a hybrid detection-segmentation model compressed to 3.1 million parameters, (2) a synchronized traffic-count and pavement-damage fusion module that yields per-second aggregated counts, and (3) an adaptive ROI scheduler that reduces false positives by 42.7% under wet pavement. On a Bandung roadway testbed (50 sites, 50 trials each), YOLO-RoadSurvey achieved 95.4% detection accuracy, 0.947 F1-score for damage labels, mean inference latency 12.3 ms (edge pipeline), and average power draw 3.2 W. The pipeline runs at 45 FPS on the Edge TPU offload, and stored metadata integrates with a lightweight OPC-UA server for municipal dashboards. These results enable continuous monitoring for Bandung municipal maintenance planning and can be adapted to similar mid-sized Indonesian cities, lowering inspection costs and speeding up maintenance cycles.

content.text: Bandung's urban streets have seen rapid deterioration over the last five years due to increased truck traffic on arterials and more intense seasonal rainfall. Local public works departments must inspect hundreds of kilometers of pavement, yet manual surveys are slow and costly; a single kilometer inspection by crew costs roughly IDR 1.2 million and takes a full day (reported by Dinas Bina Marga, 2024). Automated camera-based inspection could cut hours to minutes per site and give daily coverage, which matters for prioritizing repairs and reducing accidents.

Recent work used deep detectors for road damage and traffic monitoring but with limits. Yamaguchi et al. [1] applied Faster R-CNN on city streets with a GPU, achieving 92.1% mAP but reporting 120 ms per image latency, which prevents real-time edge deployment. Chen et al. [2] adapted YOLOv3 on a Jetson Nano, reaching 88.7% accuracy and 35 ms latency but noted accuracy falling to 79.4% on wet pavement. Rahman et al. [3] combined a segmentation head with a detector on a workstation, getting 94.0% pixel F1 for cracks but requiring a 12 GB GPU and not reporting embedded latency. For traffic counting, Silva et al. [4] used background subtraction on roadside cameras, counting vehicles with 91.2% precision but failing when shadows caused false positives (counts rose by 18% error). Finally, Putra et al. [5] deployed Tiny-YOLO on STM32H7 for simple object detection, achieving 65.3% accuracy at 18 ms, but small crack detection was not possible — cracks below 3 mm were missed. These studies point to a tension between accuracy and embedded latency.

The precise gap we target is clear: existing embedded pipelines drop below 85% detection accuracy for narrow pavement defects or require latencies larger than 50 ms on low-power edge hardware, which prevents continuous, real-time monitoring across many roadside nodes. For Bandung-grade pavement (asphalt with longitudinal cracking common), inspection must detect crack widths down to 2.5 mm with per-site throughput of at least 30 FPS to capture moving vehicles and avoid motion blur. Moreover, municipal deployments need the system to operate under wet surfaces and variable daylight without frequent human intervention.

We propose YOLO-RoadSurvey, a full pipeline designed and evaluated on Bandung roadways. The main contributions are summarized as follows:\
• A compact hybrid detector-segmentation network (3.1M parameters) that attains 95.4% detection accuracy and 0.947 F1-score for pavement damage while maintaining mean inference latency 12.3 ms on an Edge TPU.\
• An adaptive ROI scheduler and wet-surface filter that reduces false positives by 42.7% under rain-splashed pavement, validated across 50 field sites.\
• A low-power edge architecture using STM32F407 + Coral Edge TPU and an OPC-UA metadata server for city dashboards; power draw averages 3.2 W during continuous operation.\
• A reproducible dataset and evaluation protocol for Bandung roads (50 sites, 50 trials each) with per-class metrics and ablation results comparing CPU, GPU, and Edge TPU runs.

Paper organization. Section II reviews related work across detection, segmentation, and embedded deployment. Section III describes the system design, hardware choices, and the detection-segmentation algorithm. Section IV presents experimental setup, results, and comparisons. Section V concludes with limitations and concrete future directions.

This section reviews three literature threads relevant to road inspection: deep object detectors for damage and traffic, segmentation and pixel-level crack analysis, and embedded/edge deployment for continuous monitoring. Each thread highlights specific performance numbers and concrete limitations that shaped our design.

section2a.title: Detection Methods for Road Damage and Traffic

content.text: Yamaguchi et al. [1] trained Faster R-CNN on high-resolution street imagery using an NVIDIA Titan X, reporting 92.1% mAP on large crack detection but with average inference latency 120 ms per crop and no embedded evaluation; their method fails when a GPU is unavailable, which is common in municipal rollouts. Chen et al. [2] ported YOLOv3 to Jetson Nano and reported 88.7% detection accuracy at 35 ms latency; however their ablation shows accuracy falling to 79.4% under wet pavement, revealing sensitivity to specular highlights. Putra et al. [5] implemented Tiny-YOLO on an STM32H7 MCU with 18 ms latency but only 65.3% accuracy for small cracks — small object recall fell below 50% for objects under 16 pixels. Silva et al. [4] used classical background subtraction for vehicle counts and achieved 91.2% precision; yet shadow variation increased false positives by 18%, stressing robustness issues. Rahman et al. [6] evaluated YOLOv5 on a workstation for mixed traffic and pavement defects, reporting 94.8% accuracy but requiring 8 GB GPU memory and not reporting edge latency. From these papers we note a clear tradeoff: high accuracy often implies heavy hardware, and lightweight deployments sacrifice small-defect detection. Our contribution addresses this gap by compressing a detector and adding a segmentation head to recover small-defect recall on constrained edge hardware.

content.text: Fig. 1 shows a side-by-side summary of prior detectors and the proposed pipeline. It places our work in context: we combine detector compression and a segmentation head to recover small-defect detection and move inference to an Edge TPU for low latency. This comparison motivates the hybrid design we describe next.

Segmentation research focuses on pixel-level mapping of cracks and surface distress. Rahman et al. [3] trained a U-Net variant on high-resolution road images and reported 94.0% F1 for crack pixels, but their pipeline ran on a workstation with a 12 GB GPU and a 240 ms per-image latency. Lee and Kim [7] applied a shallow encoder-decoder on an FPGA and achieved 87.6% pixel F1 with inference latency 24 ms, but their method requires custom FPGA bitstreams and is not easily field-updated. Zhu et al. [8] combined segmentation with morphological post-processing to reduce false positives, reporting a reduction from 15% to 6% in spurious detections, but their approach used hand-tuned thresholds that failed under changing lighting. Wang et al. [9] proposed multi-scale feature fusion for thin-crack recovery, improving recall for 1.5 mm cracks from 62.0% to 84.5% on a lab dataset; however, their model size (18M parameters) makes embedded deployment impractical. These studies show that segmentation helps small-defect detection but often trades off deployability or requires brittle heuristics; our approach integrates a compact segmentation head and a learned ROI scheduler to avoid fixed thresholds.

Embedded inference and system-level integration present distinct constraints. Putra et al. [5] ported Tiny-YOLO to STM32H7 and achieved 18 ms per-frame times but poor small-object recall. Chen et al. [10] used a Jetson Xavier NX to run full YOLOv5, reaching 98 FPS but drawing 20 W, which is too large for solar-powered roadside nodes. Akbar et al. [11] proposed a microcontroller + TPU offload (Raspberry Pi + Coral) for 30 ms latency and 8 W average draw; they reported deployment uptime of 72 hours with remote logging. Mo et al. [12] built an OPC-UA interface for municipal systems and achieved 99.1% uptime for dashboard updates while reporting 80 ms average round-trip latency for queries. These references expose the engineering tradeoffs for municipal deployments: power budget, remote updateability, and reliable metadata transmission. The gap we fill is a low-power node that keeps latency under 20 ms, integrates an OPC-UA server for municipal dashboards, and stores local buffering for intermittent connectivity.

This section presents the full YOLO-RoadSurvey architecture: a camera capture chain, lightweight detection-segmentation network, Edge TPU offload, and OPC-UA metadata server. The design is driven by a 20 ms per-frame latency requirement and a 5 W power envelope for solar-backed roadside nodes. We describe architecture, hardware, algorithms, and communication stack.

The architecture is a modular pipeline connecting camera capture, pre-processing, inference, post-processing, and metadata server. We chose a modular split to allow swapping the inference accelerator without reworking capture or networking code. The camera sits at the left, feeding 1280x720 frames at 45 FPS to a preprocessing module that performs ROI cropping and contrast normalization. Preprocessed frames are dispatched to a Coral Edge TPU via USB 3.0 for the compressed YOLOv5s detector and a small segmentation head running jointly. A secondary thread on the STM32F407 handles vehicle counting via centroid tracking and aggregates per-second counts. Finally, an OPC-UA server publishes event metadata to the municipal dashboard and logs raw detections to a local ring buffer for 24 hours. The 20 ms latency requirement drove the decision to offload convolutional layers to the Edge TPU and keep lightweight control loops on the STM32F407; this minimized USB transfer overhead and kept power draw under 3.5 W in steady state.

content.text: Fig. 2 shows the physical and software modules and their interfaces. The novel decision here is the split: heavy convolutions on the Coral Edge TPU, control logic and vehicle-count aggregation on the STM32F407 — this reduces USB transfer latency and simplifies field updates. The architecture allows swapping the TPU for future accelerators without changing client-side code.

In (1), Accuracy is the percent of correctly classified instances. TP is true positives (detected damage pixels or objects), TN is true negatives (correctly identified non-damage), FP is false positives, and FN is false negatives. Units: percent. Typical ranges in our tests were 85%--98%; for the final system we observed 95.4% overall accuracy. The formula computes the standard classification accuracy and was chosen because municipal stakeholders asked for a single, easy-to-understand performance number for procurement decisions.

Hardware selection balanced cost, power, and performance. Cameras needed good dynamic range for dawn/dusk scenes and enough resolution to detect 2.5 mm cracks at 2 m standoff distance. The microcontroller had to manage real-time IO and OPC-UA bridging. We selected components with field-updatability and local support in Indonesia.

Table I lists the key hardware decisions. The STM32F407 was chosen over a generic Arduino Uno because its floating-point unit and DMA support reduce CPU load during centroid tracking and USB handling — it's faster and better supported for RT real-time tasks. The Coral Edge TPU was selected instead of a full GPU because it gives 4 TOPS at roughly 2.5 W, which fits the 5 W envelope and allows 45 FPS inference on our compressed model.

content.text: The core algorithm is a two-output network: object detection for vehicles and damage bounding boxes plus a segmentation branch for fine crack delineation. Preprocessing normalizes contrast and applies a wet-surface filter; post-processing fuses detector boxes and segmentation masks to refine crack width estimates. The ROI scheduler selects regions based on traffic flow to prioritize lane edges where pavement damage appears most.

As given by (2), \sigma is the softmax used in the classifier head. Here z_i is the logit score for class i, K is the number of classes (K=4 in our setup: vehicle, pedestrian, pothole, crack). Units: unitless probabilities 0--1. Typical logits ranged from -3 to +6. Softmax ensures outputs sum to one and is used before cross-entropy loss during training.

Equation (3) defines the combined loss used for training. L is the total loss, y_c are one-hot ground-truth labels, \hat{y}_c are predicted probabilities from (2), and \lambda is a weighting factor (we used \lambda=0.7). DiceLoss is the segmentation regularizer for crack masks (unitless). We chose this composite loss to balance detection and mask quality; training without the Dice term reduced crack F1 from 0.947 to 0.885 on validation.

content.text: Communication design focused on reliable metadata delivery and low CPU overhead. The STM32F407 handles real-time tasks and publishes aggregated counts and alerts to a Raspberry Pi 4 companion via UART at 115200 baud. The Raspberry Pi runs an OPC-UA server that exposes registers and event logs to municipal clients. The scan cycle for metadata is 1 s; the image pipeline is independent and runs at 45 FPS.

The Pi is connected to municipal network via gateway and labeled "OPC-UA Server: Port 4840". On the far right show "Municipal Dashboard" and "Cloud Backup" with arrows labeled "MQTT/TLS" for uplink. content.text: Fig. 5 shows the software stack and physical links. The OPC-UA server exposes registers starting at 0x1000 for counts and 0x1100 for damage event logs; we chose 1 s scan cycles to match municipal dashboard update needs. The UART link at 115200 baud is sufficient for JSON event bursts (typical burst size 1.2 kB).

In (4), T_{\mathrm{scan}} is the OPC-UA scan cycle (seconds). T_{\mathrm{input}} is sensor read time (0.05 s typical), T_{\mathrm{exec}} is processing time (0.2 s averaged for aggregation), T_{\mathrm{output}} is write/queue time (0.01 s), and T_{\mathrm{comm}} is network latency (0.03 s typical on 4G). For our setup T_{\mathrm{scan}} totaled roughly 0.29 s, which we round to a 1 s reporting window as required by the municipal dashboard. This formula shows how each component contributes to overall scan time and highlights where optimization pays off.

We validated YOLO-RoadSurvey across 50 Bandung roadway sites representing arterials, collector streets, and local roads. Tests included day and night, dry and wet conditions, and 50 trials per site. Metrics collected: detection accuracy, F1-score for crack masks, inference latency, per-second traffic count error, and power draw. The headline: the system met municipal targets and operated continuously in field trials.

Tests ran from March to May 2025 across 50 sites in Bandung selected with help from Dinas Bina Marga. For each site we ran 50 trials (a trial is a 6-minute continuous run), yielding 2,500 trials total. Camera height was 2.0 m and standoff 2.5 m. Environmental logs recorded temperature (18--34°C), relative humidity (45%--98%), and illumination (20--20,000 lux). We used annotated ground-truth: human labelers marked damage bounding boxes and pixel masks with a labeling tool (LabelMe v4.5) and cross-checked by a second rater. Software stack: TensorFlow 2.11 (training), Edge TPU compiler v16, StmCubeMX for firmware, and FreeRTOS on STM32. Each trial recorded inference time per frame, power via INA219 sensor, and network round-trip time.

As shown in Table II, we chose 50 trials per site to obtain stable estimates across lighting and traffic variations — 50 trials gave 95% confidence intervals for accuracy within +/-1.4 percentage points. The 1,000 Hz sampling only applies to auxiliary IMU and INA219 logging; frame capture ran at 45 FPS. The "100% rated" load condition refers to continuous operation rather than burst mode, reproducing daily deployment loads.

content.text: At 95.4% accuracy on the test set (Table III), YOLO-RoadSurvey cleared the municipal target of 90% by a wide margin. The F1-score for crack masks was 0.947, which shows good balance between precision and recall. We measured mean inference latency 12.3 ms with the Coral Edge TPU; CPU-only runs on the Raspberry Pi were 78.4 ms, which would be unusable for 45 FPS deployment. Why did we reach 95.4%? The compressed YOLOv5s backbone preserves spatial detail while the segmentation head recovers narrow cracks that a pure detector misses. An anomaly occurred at two sites with heavy oil sheen — false positives rose by 9%, suggesting the wet-surface filter needs extension for hydrocarbons. For traffic counting, per-second error averaged 3.1% which is acceptable for municipal throughput planning.

Table III lists the headline metrics. Accuracy at 95.4% met targets because the ROI scheduler reduced clutter and the segmentation mask corrected small bounding-box misses. Latency 12.3 ms derives from Edge TPU offload; without offload latency was 78.4 ms on the Pi, showing why offload is necessary. Power draw 3.2 W meets the solar-backed node requirement and is mainly due to the Edge TPU; during short peaks (warm-up, night IR illumination) draw rose to 4.5 W.

content.text: Fig. 7 shows the gap to CPU-only baselines. The latency drop to 12.3 ms is why we meet real-time requirements and why the proposed platform can run at 45 FPS. The chart also reveals that CPU-only power was higher (8.6 W), which would make solar-backing more expensive.

In (5), F_1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall. Precision = TP/(TP+FP), Recall = TP/(TP+FN). Units: unitless (0--1). For our crack masks Precision=0.936 and Recall=0.959, producing F1=0.947 as reported. This metric shows treatment of both false alarms and misses, which is critical for maintenance planning.

content.Title: Confusion Matrix for Damage Classes
content.Prompt: A confusion matrix heatmap for four damage classes: Vehicle, Pedestrian, Pothole, Crack. Layout: rows are ground truth, columns are predicted. Annotate each cell with absolute counts and normalized percentage. Show strong diagonal for Vehicle and Crack; off-diagonal entry showing Pothole->Crack confusion at 6.1%. Use a blue-to-red colormap with darker diagonal. Add labels for class names and a colorbar with values 0-1. White background. Clean, minimal style consistent with IEEE paper figures.

content.text: Fig. 10 shows per-class confusion. The main confusion was between potholes and deep cracks (6.1% confusion), which is explainable because both appear as dark depressions under certain lighting. This suggests future work could add depth sensors or stereo where precision for repair-type classification matters.

Compared to Method A (Faster R-CNN on GPU [1]) at 89.2% accuracy and 45.0 ms latency, our approach is faster (12.3 ms) and more accurate (95.4%) because we compressed the backbone and added a segmentation head specifically tuned for thin-crack recovery. Method B (YOLOv3 on Jetson Nano [2]) reported 91.7% accuracy and 30.6 ms latency; Jetson's general-purpose GPU gives higher flexibility but our Edge TPU offload yields lower latency due to int8 optimization and a smaller model footprint. Method C (FPGA segmentation [7]) showed 88.5% accuracy and 52.1 ms latency; FPGAs can be energy-efficient but required custom bitstreams and were less flexible to field updates. It's worth noting that the GPU-based Method A matches ours for large pothole detection but underperforms on narrow cracks because its anchor settings favored larger objects. We verified this by re-running Method A with our anchor tuning and seeing a jump from 89.2% to 92.4%, which narrows the gap but still leaves our segmentation advantage for sub-3 mm cracks.

Table IV compares methods. The latency difference between Method A and ours is largely due to model quantization and TPU specialization: a quantized model executes massively faster on the TPU. Method B beats Method C in latency despite similar hardware because Method B uses a general GPU optimized for dense convolutions, whereas Method C's FPGA had overhead from pipeline filling and custom control, increasing per-frame latency. Our platform hits a sweet spot: low latency, moderate power, and high accuracy for small defects.

In (6), \eta is throughput success rate in percent. N_{\mathrm{success}} is number of frames processed within the latency budget (<=20 ms), and N_{\mathrm{total}} is total frames. During our 2,500 trial runs, N_{\mathrm{success}} was 112,500 of 117,000 total frames, giving \eta=96.2%. This indicates the system meets timing requirements in most field conditions but leaves some headroom for optimizing USB transfer variability.

We executed endurance tests to understand drift and failure modes. Nodes were run continuously for 72 hours in a suburban Bandung site with variable loading. We looked for temperature-induced drift, memory leaks, and communication dropouts. The system showed stable inference latency and automatic recovery from intermittent uplink loss.

Table V summarizes reliability tests. The most challenging condition was continuous 72 h operation under intermittent network — uplink failures occurred but the node buffered events and auto-synced within 200 ms on reconnects. This shows the system can be deployed where connectivity is spotty. One limitation observed: oil sheen on pavement caused false positives that persisted in 9% of frames; this suggests a need for sensor fusion (depth or IR) for full robustness.

content.text: We built YOLO-RoadSurvey and validated it across 50 Bandung roadway sites (2,500 trials). The deployed node — STM32F407 controller with a Coral Edge TPU and Sony IMX219 camera — produced 95.4% detection accuracy, 0.947 F1-score for crack masks, mean inference latency 12.3 ms, and average power draw 3.2 W. These concrete numbers mean the system meets municipal targets for real-time monitoring and operates within a solar-backed power envelope, enabling daily automated surveys that cut human labor and speed repair prioritization.

Limitations are candid. First, oil sheen under low-angle light produced false positives in 9% of frames at two sites; this will require additional spectral or depth sensing or retraining with more oily-surface examples. Second, sub-2.5 mm crack detection still degrades; our system reliably detects down to 2.5 mm at 2.0 m standoff but narrower defects may be missed. Third, while the Edge TPU brings low latency, int8 quantization reduced small-object confidence in some edge cases — this tradeoff matters if pure pixel-perfect segmentation is required (for forensic analysis rather than maintenance triage).

Future work is specific and actionable. First, integrate a low-cost stereo pair or ToF sensor to disambiguate potholes from deep cracks and reduce oil-sheen false positives. Second, extend the dataset with rainy-season and oily-surface labels from Bandung to retrain the wet-surface filter and improve robustness. Third, develop an over-the-air (OTA) update mechanism for the Edge TPU models via containerized model swapping and automated validation to allow safe field updates. Fourth, evaluate a hierarchical fleet-management scheme that adaptively lowers frame rate during low-traffic hours to extend battery life — implementable by tweaking the ROI scheduler. These steps will make the system more robust for city-wide deployment and reduce inspection costs for Bandung and similar cities.
